source: NMC MD Pharmacology guideline 2022; RangDale9 ch2, ch8; KDT8 ch4, ch6; Sarkar OCR; unsourced items marked

cards.front: What does the NMC long exercise in the MD Pharmacology practical exam consist of?
cards.back: Three kinds of task: designing a protocol for a given scenario, auditing a given case, and performing an experiment or a simulated experiment. The examiner watches the exercise, notes how the candidate responds and assesses it, and may ask questions on it. The practical exam runs over two days and mainly tests the psychomotor domain.
refs: WEB NMC Guidelines for Competency Based PG Training Programme for MD in Pharmacology 01-08-2022 (owner copy: design/NMC-MD-Pharmacology-2022.txt)

cards.front: Short note: Isolated organ bath set-up for a tissue experiment

points: A strip of tissue is suspended in an organ bath and its contraction or relaxation is recorded
Responses at increasing concentrations give a concentration-effect curve
Tissue bathed in a physiological salt solution chosen for the tissue
Solution aerated (oxygen or air) and held at a constant temperature
Fixed resting tension and a stabilisation period before dosing
Tissue tied to a lever or force transducer
Response written on a kymograph or physiograph (the NMC lists organ bath and physiograph among required equipment)
Agonist potency and maximal response
Antagonist affinity by dose ratio and Schild analysis
Screening for specific activity

refs: WEB NMC Guidelines for Competency Based PG Training Programme for MD in Pharmacology 01-08-2022 (owner copy: design/NMC-MD-Pharmacology-2022.txt)

cards.front: Guinea pig ileum: what is it used to show in the practical exam?
cards.back: Acetylcholine contracts it through muscarinic receptors, and atropine blocks this response. Histamine contracts it through H1 receptors; the guinea pig ileum responds far more than human ileum and remains the standard tissue for histamine bioassay.

cards.front: Frog rectus abdominis: which receptor does it test, and what phenomenon does it show?
cards.back: Nicotinic receptors of skeletal muscle (the end plate). Repeated or large doses of acetylcholine give smaller and smaller contractions, and the response recovers only after a rest: this is receptor desensitisation.

cards.front: Rat isolated gastric fundus: which 5-HT receptor mediates its contraction?
cards.back: 5-HT2B receptor. The 5-HT2 receptor subtypes all couple to Gq, activate phospholipase C and generate IP3 and DAG; contraction of the rat gastric fundus is mediated by 5-HT2B.

cards.front: Short note: Langendorff isolated perfused heart

points: Heart removed from an anaesthetised animal; aorta tied to a cannula
Oxygenated buffer (usually Krebs-Henseleit, 37 °C, pH 7.4) flows backwards into the aorta, shuts the aortic valve and enters the coronary arteries
The heart keeps beating without nerves or circulation
The rat heart is the best-characterised small-heart model; large hearts are costly and variable
Heart rate
Contractile force (isometric transducer)
Coronary flow
Left ventricular pressure (balloon in the ventricle)
Positive and negative inotropes (e.g. isoprenaline effect blocked by a beta-blocker)
Coronary dilators; calcium antagonism after barium chloride spasm
Antiarrhythmic and antifibrillatory testing
Ischaemia-reperfusion studies

cards.front: Langendorff heart: constant-flow versus constant-pressure perfusion.
cards.back: Constant flow: a pump fixes the flow, and changes in coronary perfusion pressure are measured; good for low-flow ischaemia and vasoactive drugs, but it overrides coronary autoregulation. Constant pressure: reservoir height (or feedback) fixes the pressure, so flow follows the heart's demand and autoregulation is kept; good for ischaemia-reperfusion work, but vascular reactivity is harder to measure.

cards.front: Essay: Recording a dose-response curve of acetylcholine on an isolated tissue (step-wise)

points: State the aim (graded DRC of ACh; effect of an antagonist if asked)
Animal use approved by the institutional animal ethics committee
Sacrifice humanely, dissect the tissue quickly into aerated salt solution
Tie the tissue to the bath hook and the lever or transducer; set resting tension
Let it stabilise with regular washes
Add doses in increasing order on a fixed time cycle
Keep contact time constant, then wash out and wait before the next dose
Repeat doses to check reproducibility
Measure the height of each contraction
Express as percent of maximum and plot against log dose: a sigmoid curve
Read EC50 from the curve
Avoid overstretching or touching the tissue
Keep temperature and aeration constant
Use fresh solutions; avoid air bubbles and spillage

cards.front: Why is a dose-response curve plotted on a log-dose scale?
cards.back: On a linear dose scale the curve is a rectangular hyperbola, because drug-receptor binding follows the law of mass action. On a log-dose scale it becomes sigmoid, with a near-linear middle part (about 30 to 70% response). This spreads out the useful range and makes curves easy to compare.

cards.front: Define EC50 and relative potency.
cards.back: EC50 is the concentration that gives half the maximal response. Relative potency compares two agonists by the doses that give the same response, usually their EC50s: a curve lying further right means a less potent drug.

cards.front: Define pD2 and pA2.
cards.back: pD2: the negative log of the molar EC50 of an agonist; a higher pD2 means a more potent agonist. pA2: the negative log of the molar concentration of an antagonist that makes it necessary to double the agonist concentration to get the original response (dose ratio 2). pA2 measures antagonist affinity. The NMC expects candidates to determine EC50, ED50, pD2 and pA2.
refs: WEB NMC Guidelines for Competency Based PG Training Programme for MD in Pharmacology 01-08-2022 (owner copy: design/NMC-MD-Pharmacology-2022.txt)

cards.front: How do competitive and noncompetitive antagonists change an agonist's log dose-response curve?
cards.back: Competitive: parallel shift to the right with the same maximum, because enough agonist overcomes the block (surmountable). Noncompetitive: the antagonist acts at another site, so even high agonist concentrations cannot fully reverse it; the curve is flattened and the maximum falls.

cards.front: Complete: Schild analysis of a competitive antagonist
cards.text: The dose ratio (r) is the factor by which agonist concentration must be raised to restore a response in the presence of the antagonist. Plot {{log (r - 1)}} against {{log antagonist concentration}}; for a simple competitive antagonist this gives a straight line, and its intercept on the {{x-axis}} gives the antagonist dissociation constant {{KB}}.

cards.front: In a tracing exercise, how do you identify an unknown agonist on guinea pig ileum?
cards.back: Compare it with known agonists and test which selective antagonist blocks it. If atropine blocks the response, it acts on muscarinic receptors (an ACh-like drug); if an H1 blocker such as mepyramine blocks it, it is histamine-like. A parallel right shift points to competitive block.

cards.front: Define bioassay. Why is a standard always run with the unknown?
cards.back: Bioassay estimates the concentration or potency of a substance from the biological response it produces. Biological systems vary between laboratories and over time, so absolute units are unreliable; comparing the unknown with a standard on the same preparation gives a relative potency that different laboratories can agree on.

cards.front: Classify: designs of bioassay on isolated tissue
cards.text: In order of rising accuracy: {{matching (single-point)}} assay, {{bracketing}} assay, {{graphical interpolation}} assay, {{three-point (2 + 1)}} assay, {{four-point (2 + 2)}} assay and multiple-point assays.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual (Bikash Medhi), PDF p73 (printed p57): bracketing, matching, interpolation, multiple-point

cards.front: Matching (single-point) bioassay: principle, merit and drawback.
cards.back: A fixed dose of the test is given, and doses of the standard are tried until one gives an equal response; the two doses are taken as equipotent. Merit: simple and quick. Drawbacks: least accurate, assumes the tissue sensitivity is constant, and gives no estimate of error.

cards.front: Bracketing bioassay: principle and use.
cards.back: The test response is placed between two standard responses, one just above and one just below it, and potency is found by interpolating between them. It copes with slow drift in tissue sensitivity better than matching, but still gives no measure of error.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual (Bikash Medhi), PDF p75 (printed p59): response bracketed between two standard responses
Ghosh Fundamentals of Experimental Pharmacology PDF p92-93: matching or bracketing assay

cards.front: Graphical interpolation bioassay: how is potency read?
cards.back: A full log dose-response curve of the standard is drawn first. The test is then given and its response read off the linear part of the standard curve to find the equivalent standard dose. It needs a stable tissue, because the curve is built before the test is given.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual (Bikash Medhi), PDF p75-76 (printed p59-60): response read from standard dose-response plot

cards.front: Short note: Three-point (2 + 1) bioassay

points: Two doses of standard (S1, S2) and one dose of test (T), all on the linear part of the log DRC
Test response should fall between the two standard responses
Doses given in randomised order (e.g. a Latin square) and repeated
Fixed contact time and time cycle with washes between doses
Potency read from where the test response lies on the line joining S1 and S2 on a log-dose scale
Only one test dose, so parallelism of standard and test cannot be checked

refs: Medhi Practical Manual (Bikash Medhi), PDF p76-77 (printed p60-61): three-point assay, s1 and s2 standard doses

cards.front: Short note: Four-point (2 + 2) parallel-line bioassay

points: Two doses each of standard and unknown (S1, S2, U1, U2) on the linear part of the log DRC
Simplest parallel-line assay
Doses repeated in random order
Repetition gives a built-in measure of variability
Potency ratio from the horizontal distance between the two parallel lines
Statistics give confidence limits of the estimate
Checks that the two lines are parallel
More reliable than matching, bracketing or three-point assays

cards.front: What are the main sources of error in bioassay, and how does the design control them?
cards.back: The main problem is biological variation. Good design minimises variation, avoids systematic error and estimates the limits of error. In practice: randomise the order of doses, keep the observer (and in human assays the subject) unaware of the dose, keep contact time, time cycle and washing fixed, and watch for tissue fatigue or desensitisation.

cards.front: When can a simple potency ratio NOT be given in a bioassay?
cards.back: When the log dose-response lines of standard and unknown are not parallel, or their maximal responses differ. This happens when the two act by different mechanisms or one is a partial agonist. A single ratio then cannot describe their relative activity.

cards.front: Morphine versus codeine: what does the human 2 + 2 analgesic assay show?
cards.back: Four patients each received high and low doses of both drugs in random order, blinded, with pain relief scored by a trained observer. Morphine was about 13 times as potent as codeine. This shows only that less morphine is needed for the same effect, not that it is the better drug.

cards.front: Where is bioassay still important today?
cards.back: Measuring activity of new or chemically undefined substances; studying endogenous mediators (e.g. cascade superfusion for short-lived mediators such as prostacyclin and nitric oxide); measuring toxicity; and standardising biopharmaceuticals (vaccines, monoclonal antibodies, recombinant proteins) that vary from batch to batch. Measuring drug levels in body fluids has largely moved to chemical analysis.

cards.front: Essay: Designing a clinical trial protocol for a given scenario (exam approach)

points: Title, protocol number and date; sponsor; investigators and sites
Project summary of no more than about 300 words that stands alone
Why the study is needed (the problem and the gap)
Primary objective, then secondary objectives: simple, specific and fixed in advance
Type of study and phase; randomisation, blinding and control
Study population with inclusion, exclusion and withdrawal criteria; expected duration
Interventions, procedures, measurements and lab tests
Patient information sheet and written informed consent
Stopping rules and a flow chart
Adverse-event recording and reporting; follow-up
Sample size, data management and analysis plan; quality assurance
Ethics section and consent forms in English and local language
Budget, insurance, conflict of interest, publication policy

cards.front: How should the objectives of a research protocol be written?
cards.back: Simple rather than complex, specific rather than vague, and stated before the research starts. The primary objective comes first; secondary objectives follow. Goals describe what the proposal hopes to achieve; objectives state the research questions.

cards.front: Which part of a protocol is the most important, and what must it contain?
cards.back: The methodology. It gives the interventions, procedures, measurements, observations and lab tests; selection criteria and study population; the information sheet and consent process; and, for a randomised trial, randomisation, blinding and stopping rules.

cards.front: Essay: ADR causality assessment exercise for a given case

points: Suspected drug(s), dose, dates started and stopped
Time of onset of the event; other drugs, disease and other possible causes
Temporal relationship to the drug
Previous knowledge: is the reaction known for this drug?
Dechallenge: did it subside on stopping?
Rechallenge: did it recur on re-exposure (often unethical, so rarely done)?
Naranjo algorithm: total score of 9 or more definite, 5-8 probable, 1-4 possible, 0 or less doubtful
WHO-UMC scale categories
Grade severity with the modified Hartwig scale
State the causality grade and severity
Manage the patient; report to the ADR monitoring centre under PvPI

cards.front: How does KD Tripathi grade the causality of an adverse event?
cards.back: Definite: causality proven. Probable: not proven, but the drug is the likely cause. Possible: the drug or other causes could be responsible. Doubtful: the drug is unlikely to be the cause but cannot be ruled out.

cards.front: List the WHO-UMC causality categories.
cards.back: Certain; probable; possible; unlikely; unclassified; unclassifiable.
refs: WEB Indian J Pharmacol Agreement between Naranjo algorithm and WHO-UMC criteria for causality assessment 2014 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3912795/

cards.front: Case audit exercise: what do you check in a given case and its treatment?
cards.back: Whether each drug is indicated for the diagnosis; whether drug, dose, route, frequency and duration are right for this patient; contraindications, interactions and duplication; unnecessary or irrational combinations; generic versus brand and cost; and whether information and monitoring were planned. WHO criteria: right indication, medicine, dose and duration, patient, dispensing and adherence.
refs: WEB NMC Guidelines for Competency Based PG Training Programme for MD in Pharmacology 01-08-2022 (owner copy: design/NMC-MD-Pharmacology-2022.txt)

cards.front: What are the five steps of critical appraisal in evidence-based medicine?
cards.back: 1) Ask an answerable question (PICO: population, intervention, comparison, outcome). 2) Search for the evidence. 3) Appraise the methods and design. 4) Appraise the results. 5) Judge the significance of the results and their impact on practice.

cards.front: Essay: Critical appraisal of a published paper, section by section

points: Is the research question clear (population, intervention, outcome)?
Is the need explained, and is the hypothesis stated in advance?
Design suited to the question; inclusion and exclusion criteria; end points set beforehand
Randomisation, blinding and sources of bias
Sample size calculation and level of significance
Statistical tests suit the data (non-parametric for non-normal data)
All participants accounted for, including drop-outs and withdrawals (flow chart)
Appropriate summary measures; results match the abstract
Effect size with confidence intervals, not P values alone
Limitations and external validity discussed
Findings compared with earlier studies
Conclusions follow from the results
Funding source and conflict of interest declared and managed
Relevance to one's own patients

cards.front: Why should a paper report confidence intervals and not only P values?
cards.back: A P value only tells whether the null hypothesis is rejected. A confidence interval shows the direction and size of the effect and how precise the estimate is, so clinical importance can be judged.

cards.front: Classify: reporting guidelines used to appraise papers
cards.text: {{CONSORT}} for randomised trials (25-item checklist and flow diagram); {{PRISMA}} for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (27 items); {{STROBE}} for cohort, case-control and cross-sectional studies (22 items); {{STARD}} for diagnostic accuracy studies; {{MOOSE}} for meta-analyses of observational studies; {{SPIRIT}} for trial protocols.

cards.front: How well do the Naranjo and WHO-UMC causality scales agree?
cards.back: Poorly overall, in one Indian comparison. Agreement was highest for the 'possible' category and absent for 'certain'. Both are widely used pharmacovigilance tools.
refs: WEB Indian J Pharmacol Agreement between Naranjo algorithm and WHO-UMC criteria for causality assessment 2014 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3912795/

cards.front: Why are participants randomised in a clinical trial?
cards.back: Random allocation gives every participant an equal chance of being put in each group, so the groups are similar at baseline. This removes selection bias and protects against accidental bias that could distort the result.

cards.front: What are the three main classes of bioassay?
cards.back: Direct end-point assay, quantal (all-or-none) assay and graded assay. Graded assays include bracketing, matching, interpolation and multiple-point designs.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual PDF p73 (printed p57)

cards.front: What does an analytical dilution assay measure?
cards.back: The potency of an unknown agonist as the factor by which it is diluted or concentrated relative to a standard of the same drug. Because both are the same drug, results are similar whatever tissue, species or method is used.

cards.front: How is a 3-point bioassay set up?
cards.back: Pick three graded responses: two of the standard (S1, S2) and one of the test (T), each between 25% and 75% of maximal. Arrange them in a Latin square. Relative potency comes from the sideways displacement of the parallel log dose-response lines.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual PDF p76-77 (printed p60-61)

cards.front: How does a 4-point assay differ from a 3-point assay?
cards.back: It uses two standard and two test responses, all taken from the dose-response curves and arranged in a Latin square. It is more sensitive than the 3-point design and reduces variability.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual PDF p78 (printed p62)

cards.front: What is pA2?
cards.back: The negative log10 of the molar antagonist concentration that gives a dose ratio of 2, i.e. a two-fold shift of the agonist dose-response curve. pA10 uses the same idea at a dose ratio of 10.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual PDF p80 (printed p64)
Medhi Practical Manual PDF p81 (printed p65)

cards.front: How do pA2 and pA10 values show competitive antagonism?
cards.back: For competitive antagonism, pA2 minus pA10 should be about 0.95 (Medhi accepts 0.8 to 1.20). In Ghosh's rat seminal vesicle example, values of 0.99 and 1.19 were judged in good agreement with 0.95.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual PDF p81 (printed p65)

cards.front: What are the steps to build a Schild plot?
cards.back: 1) Plot log dose-response curves without and with antagonist. 2) Get the dose ratio (DR) at each antagonist concentration. 3) Plot log(DR minus 1) against log molar antagonist concentration (or its negative). The x-intercept gives pA2; a slope near 1 fits competitive antagonism.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual PDF p81 (printed p65)

cards.front: What does a pA2 pattern across histamine and acetylcholine tell you?
cards.back: Each antagonist is scored on guinea-pig ileum against both agonists. A high value means high specificity. A nearly flat line means the antagonist does not tell them apart (pethidine); a steep line means sharp discrimination (mepyramine, atropine).

cards.front: Why is guinea-pig ileum used to assay histamine?
cards.back: It is highly sensitive to histamine, which acts mainly on H1 receptors in the ileum. Atropine is added to the bath to improve specificity for histamine; mepyramine is added when assaying ACh.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual PDF p168 (printed p152)

cards.front: How is the guinea-pig ileum prepared for the bath?
cards.back: Fast the animal 24-48 hours and stun it. Open the abdomen and find the ileum about 10 cm before the caecum. Cut 2-3 cm, trim the mesentery, and tie it to the hook and lever in the direction it lies in the body. Relax it in Tyrode before use (Medhi gives 30-45 min for rat ileum, changing the solution 3-4 times).
refs: Medhi Practical Manual PDF p168-169 (printed p152-153)
Medhi Practical Manual PDF p86 (printed p70)

cards.front: How do you scale a drug concentration to the organ bath volume?
cards.back: The tissue sees the stock concentration scaled down to the bath volume (10, 20, 50 or 100 ml). Example: 0.2 x 10^-7 M in a 10 ml bath reaches the tissue as 0.2 x 10^-8 M. Apply the same scaling to every concentration in the set.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual PDF p85 (printed p69)

cards.front: Why avoid very high doses of a drug on one tissue preparation?
cards.back: High drug concentrations can cause tachyphylaxis: the tissue loses sensitivity and may stay contracted, so later responses are unreliable.
refs: Medhi Practical Manual PDF p168 (printed p152)
